r: This English-taught survey examines France's geography, history, and language, then explores Francophone cultures worldwide through discussion, readings, and cultural-analysis activities; no French-language production is assessed. Because instruction and assignments occur in English, the applied work is closer to introductory humanities synthesis than translation: summarizing cultural material, comparing regional practices, and producing short written reflections. Task-exposure research finds writing and synthesis positively associated with exposure, and observed-usage data shows office and writing tasks are already common AI use cases, so some erosion is plausible even this early. However, diffusion into general-education humanities sections remains uneven, and the course carries a dual GT-Pathways designation, Arts and Humanities plus Global Diversity, that anchors it in the statutory transfer core. At 24 months, actual classroom-level adoption is limited enough that the instrumental need to take the course for its transfer function persists. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI tools will competently draft cultural comparisons, historical syntheses, and discussion prompts of the kind this course assigns, and productivity research on professional writing, faster output paired with quality gains, suggests students and instructors alike will lean on such tools for exactly these deliverables. Because the course requires no oral or written French production, embodiment offers no protection, unlike francophone-language courses elsewhere in this batch; the content is fully digital and text-based. What still anchors the rating is the GT-Pathways general-studies designation, which caps erosion at Medium rather than allowing a rise to High, since transfer-core credit continues routing students through the course regardless of how AI-assisted individual assignments become. The instrumental case for taking the course specifically for cross-cultural content weakens, but the transfer requirement sustains partial necessity. Rating: Medium, with moderate confidence given the course's unusually generic humanities framing.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating fluent cross-cultural and historical synthesis on demand, comparable to how history-survey general-education courses read elsewhere in this framework: no embodiment, no verification-critical stakes, and no accreditation lock beyond the GT-Pathways designation. The instrumental rationale for a student to personally produce the comparative cultural analysis this course assigns is substantially eroded by 2036 under the central capability trajectory, and the course's dual general-studies designation is the only structural element still requiring enrollment. The rating holds at Medium rather than rising further because that statutory transfer-core mandate does not disappear on this horizon even as course content becomes trivially automatable. Confidence is moderate-to-low: ten-year forecasts for how gen-ed humanities electives evolve are inherently uncertain, and GT-Pathways requirements could themselves be revised, removing the one factor still protecting this course.
FRE 1001.d: In this course taught in English, students explore the vibrant cultures of France and of the French-speaking world. In the first part of the course, students examine France as a nation defined by elements of geographical boundaries, history, and language. The second part explores the French-speaking cultures around the world. Built as a cross-cultural journey, the course presents contemporary issues via culturally responsive materials and engaging activities. While broadening their knowledge, students familiarize themselves with a variety of cultural values and ways of living. Students should consider taking FRE 1010 for an even richer experience.

r: Elementary French I builds beginning listening, speaking, reading, and writing through functional communicative activities and cultural-competency content, foundational skill acquisition rather than a translation task itself. This is a genuine hard case: task-exposure research classifies translators and interpreters among the most-exposed occupations, which pushes down the instrumental case for learning a language purely to move between languages. But the course's aim is the student's own oral proficiency, part of it embodied real-time speaking practice, and it carries a GT-Pathways Oral Communication designation gating the statutory transfer core. At 24 months, the existence of fluent machine translation does not erode the instrumental need for a student to acquire personal communicative competence in French, nor does it touch the general-education mandate the course satisfies. Rating: Low, matching the pattern established for equivalent elementary-language courses in this batch.

By 2031, real-time AI translation and conversational interpretation will be excellent and widely diffused, seriously eroding the instrumental rationale for learning French specifically to translate, read foreign text, or handle basic cross-language tasks, exactly the downward pressure task-exposure research on translators signals. What survives is the value of embodied, real-time interpersonal communication where a student speaks the language directly rather than routing through a device, plus the course's GT-Pathways Oral Communication designation and its role as prerequisite scaffolding for FRE 1020 and the broader sequence. Those two protections, embodiment and institutional lock, cap the erosion at Medium rather than allowing collapse to High. The rating rises from Low to Medium: translation-as-task is largely automatable, but personal communicative competence and the transfer requirement keep the course instrumentally relevant to a meaningful degree.

A decade out, seamless AI translation is pervasive and the instrumental case for language study as a substitute for translation tools is substantially eroded, one of the clearer such examples in the catalog. What remains is direct human communication in French for interpersonal, cultural, and real-time contexts where an embodied speaker matters, plus the enduring GT-Pathways transfer requirement and the course's foundational role feeding the elementary-intermediate sequence. The rating holds at Medium rather than rising to High because embodied communicative practice and the statutory general-studies mandate both persist under the central-case forecast. Confidence is lower than for most courses in this batch: this is precisely the kind of case where reasonable analysts could argue for stronger erosion given how far machine translation may advance, and the ten-year trajectory for real-time spoken interpretation is genuinely uncertain.
FRE 1010.d: This course focuses on skills development in listening, speaking, reading, and writing with emphasis on the use of functional, communicative language for oral and written proficiency and cultural competency.

r: Elementary French II continues the skills-development sequence begun in FRE 1010, building listening, speaking, reading, and writing toward functional communicative and cultural competency. Like its predecessor, the course sits in a genuine hard case: task-exposure research ranks translators and interpreters among the most AI-exposed occupations, pressuring the instrumental case for language study downward when the underlying task is cross-language transfer. But this course's target is the student's own communicative capacity, including embodied real-time speaking practice, and it carries a GT-Pathways designation, Arts and Humanities, Global Diversity, anchoring it in the transfer core. It is also the direct prerequisite for FRE 2010, giving it scaffolding weight within the language sequence. At 24 months, machine translation's maturity does not erode the instrumental need for a student to personally build communicative competence or satisfy these requirements. Rating: Low.

By 2031, ubiquitous real-time AI translation will meaningfully erode the instrumental rationale for studying French to perform translation or simple cross-language communication, mirroring the pressure task-exposure research documents for translators generally. What is preserved is the embodied, real-time interpersonal competence the course cultivates directly, its GT-Pathways general-studies designation, and its function as scaffolding into FRE 2010 and the broader sequence, three protections that together cap the erosion at Medium. Observed-usage data shows writing and language tasks are already common AI use cases, so students will likely lean on AI for auxiliary work like vocabulary drilling or grammar checking, but the course's instrumental core, personal spoken proficiency, is not substitutable. The rating rises to Medium: translation-as-task is largely automated, yet embodied communication and institutional lock-in keep the course meaningfully necessary.

A decade out, AI-mediated translation is expected to be near-seamless, substantially eroding the instrumental case for language coursework aimed at cross-language transfer, the clearest erosion vector in this batch. What endures is the value of a student directly producing and understanding spoken and written French in real interpersonal settings, together with the GT-Pathways transfer designation and the course's continuing role as scaffolding for FRE 2010 and beyond. The rating holds at Medium rather than climbing to High because embodied communicative competence and the prerequisite and general-studies lock both persist in the central case. Confidence is lower than for most non-language courses in this batch: forecasting a decade of progress in real-time spoken machine interpretation is uncertain, and a plausible alternative reading would show more erosion than this rating reflects.
FRE 1020.d: This course is a continuation of FRE 1010 and focuses on skills development in listening, speaking, reading, and writing with emphasis on the use of functional, communicative language for oral and written proficiency and cultural competency.

r: This one-credit companion to FRE 1020 adds a professional dimension to elementary French: communicating in career-relevant situations and developing intercultural competence for cross-cultural workplace interaction. The applied task, professional and intercultural communication, sits close to the translation and interpretation work that task-exposure research ranks among the most AI-exposed activities, which weighs against the course's instrumental necessity. But the course explicitly targets a student's own capacity to communicate and navigate cultural difference in real professional encounters, an embodied and interpersonal skill, and it carries a GT-Pathways Arts and Humanities designation tying it to the transfer core. As a corequisite bolt-on to FRE 1020, it also inherits that course's scaffolding role. At 24 months, machine-translation capability does not substitute for the personal intercultural competence this course builds, nor does it remove the general-studies requirement. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI translation and cross-cultural communication assistance will be strong enough that the instrumental case for taking a dedicated course to handle routine career-relevant language tasks weakens substantially, consistent with task-exposure findings that place translators and interpreters near the top of exposed occupations. What is preserved is the course's focus on a student's own embodied intercultural competence in live professional interactions, which AI mediation does not replace, along with its GT-Pathways Arts and Humanities designation. Those two factors cap the erosion at Medium instead of allowing it to reach High. Given the course's narrow one-credit scope, its instrumental contribution was always modest, but what remains, direct human intercultural fluency on the job, is not something a translation tool substitutes for. Rating: Medium.

A decade out, workplace AI translation and cultural-context tools are expected to be highly capable and broadly diffused, further eroding the instrumental rationale for coursework aimed at career-relevant language tasks specifically. What survives is the course's emphasis on a student directly developing intercultural competence and communicating without full reliance on mediating technology, plus its continuing GT-Pathways transfer designation. The rating holds at Medium rather than rising to High because embodied interpersonal skill and the general-studies lock persist under the central-case forecast. Confidence is lower than average: this narrow, applied one-credit course has limited comparable precedent in the catalog, and a reasonable alternate reading could see it erode further toward High if workplace AI-mediated communication becomes fully normalized well before 2036.
FRE 1021.d: This one-credit course complements the existing FRE 1020 - Elementary French II or its equivalent. It adds a professional dimension to the study of French, with two main objectives: enhancing students' ability to communicate in specific, career- relevant situations in the target language, and developing intercultural expertise for effective communication with individuals from diverse cultural backgrounds.

r: This variable-credit course recognizes an approved study-abroad experience for first-year students, crediting immersive French speaking, comprehension, reading, and writing development in situ. The applied work is not classroom exercises but live, embodied, real-time communication in an authentic French-speaking environment, navigating daily life, coursework, and social interaction entirely in the target language and culture. Task-exposure research consistently places manual, physical, and real-time interpersonal work in the low-exposure category, and immersive study abroad is close to a limiting case of that: presence itself is the mechanism of learning, not information transfer that AI could intercept. No AI system can supply lived, embodied immersion or the spontaneous interpersonal negotiation it requires. At 24 months, the instrumental need for a student to physically be in a French-speaking environment to earn this credit is entirely untouched by translation-tool capability. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI translation apps will be common travel companions, potentially reducing daily friction for students abroad, but that convenience does not substitute for the course's actual credited activity: sustained immersive engagement with the language and culture in a real environment. The verification burden and embodiment factors here sit near their floor, precisely the physical, real-time, in-person category that task-exposure research and the jagged-frontier literature treat as most resistant to AI substitution, since no model can be physically present for a student. Diffusion of translation aids may change how immersion feels day to day, but it does not remove the pedagogical requirement of the embodied experience itself, nor any credit-recognition structure behind it. The instrumental case for the course remains essentially intact. Rating: Low, with the caveat that the character of immersion may shift as ambient AI translation becomes routine.

A decade out, ubiquitous real-time translation could make cross-cultural travel logistically easier, and one might imagine AI reducing the felt necessity of language proficiency for basic transactions abroad. But this course's instrumental function is not transactional translation, it is a credited, embodied immersion experience that by design requires physical presence, sustained real-time interpersonal engagement, and cultural navigation a remote system cannot perform. The central capability trajectory, even under aggressive assumptions about translation quality, does not eliminate the need for a student to be there. The genuine uncertainty is about how the study-abroad experience is used and framed pedagogically, not about whether physical immersion remains necessary to earn this credit. Rating: Low, held with lower-than-typical confidence only because this is a thin, generic variable-credit description rather than a detailed syllabus.
FRE 1800.d: This is a variable-credit course, designed for first-year students learning French in a study abroad setting. Recognizes approved study-abroad educational experience in French speaking, comprehension, reading, and writing.

r: Intermediate French I continues skills development in listening, speaking, reading, and writing, conducted mostly in French with interactive activities aimed at productive communicative use, directly analogous to the elementary sequence's translation-adjacent hard case. Task-exposure research ranks translators and interpreters among the most AI-exposed occupations, and unlike the elementary courses in this batch, FRE 2010 carries no GT-Pathways general-studies designation to anchor it in the statutory transfer core, removing one of the strongest institutional protections available elsewhere in the catalog. What remains protective is the embodied, real-time oral-communication component of the interactive classroom activities, plus the course's role as a prerequisite for FRE 2020. At 24 months, near-term diffusion into intermediate-level language instruction is still limited, and the prerequisite scaffolding keeps enrollment necessary even as translation tools mature. Rating: Medium.

By 2031, AI translation and conversational-practice tools will be highly capable and widely adopted, and because this course lacks a GT-Pathways designation, the institutional floor that caps erosion for FRE 1010 and FRE 1020 does not apply here. The prerequisite-scaffolding protection this course offers is defined to cap erosion only at the 24-month horizon under the deterministic rule, so it no longer holds back the rating at five years. Task-exposure research's placement of translation and interpretation among the most-exposed activities, combined with productivity findings on how quickly professional writing and language tasks absorb AI assistance, points toward substantial erosion of the instrumental case for taking this specific course to build intermediate French skills, even though embodied oral practice still occurs in class. Rating: High, reflecting the absence of a durable institutional anchor at this horizon.

A decade out, near-seamless AI translation and conversational interpretation are the central-case expectation, and without a GT-Pathways designation or an accreditation-level lock, little structural protection remains for this specific course beyond its place in the French major and minor sequence, a program requirement rather than a broad transfer mandate, which the rubric treats as weak protection alone. The embodied oral-communication practice within the classroom is real but does not, on its own, prevent the rating from rising once the institutional caps lapse. Rating: High, hedged substantially: ten-year forecasts of language-classroom AI adoption are uncertain, embodied real-time speaking practice retains some protective value a purely task-based reading might understate, and this rating could look too aggressive if intermediate-language study remains valued for reasons the instrumental framework does not fully capture.
FRE 2010.d: This course is the first of a two-semester, integrated, second-year sequence. The course focuses on further skills development in listening, speaking, reading, and writing, with emphasis on the use of functional, communicative language for oral and written proficiency and on cultural competency. Class is conducted mostly in French and will include a variety of interactive activities designed to help students develop their knowledge of French and their ability to use it productively in situations of communication.

r: Intermediate French II continues the second-year sequence begun in FRE 2010, developing listening, speaking, reading, and writing in a mostly French-conducted classroom with interactive communicative activities. As with FRE 2010, the underlying skill, cross-language communicative competence, sits in the translation-adjacent hard case that task-exposure research flags as highly exposed for professional translators and interpreters, and this course likewise carries no GT-Pathways designation to anchor it institutionally. What protects the rating at 24 months is the embodied, real-time oral-practice component built into interactive classroom work, together with the course's function as the gateway prerequisite into FRE 3010 and further upper-division French study. Near-term diffusion of AI language tools into intermediate coursework remains partial, and the prerequisite chain keeps the instrumental need for enrollment intact for now. Rating: Medium.

By 2031, mature AI translation and conversational tools substantially erode the instrumental rationale for taking a dedicated course to build intermediate communicative competence, and the absence of a GT-Pathways designation here means no transfer-core mandate offsets that erosion. The prerequisite-scaffolding protection this course provides toward FRE 3010 caps the rating at Medium only at the 24-month horizon under the deterministic rule, so it no longer restrains the five-year rating. Task-exposure research's consistent placement of translation and interpretation among the most AI-exposed activities, together with fast-moving capability trends in real-time spoken language processing, supports a rise to High: the applied communicative task is competently performed by AI for most practical purposes, even as some embodied classroom practice continues. Rating: High, with the course's continuing prerequisite role a real but structurally limited offset.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing real-time spoken and written translation at a level that substantially displaces the instrumental need to build intermediate communicative competence specifically to communicate across languages. FRE 2020 lacks the GT-Pathways anchor that protects the elementary sequence, and its role feeding FRE 3010 is a program-internal requirement rather than a broad institutional lock, which the rubric treats as weak protection at this horizon. Embodied, in-class oral practice persists as a genuine residual value, but it does not by itself hold the rating below High once the structural caps lapse. Rating: High, hedged considerably: predicting a decade of progress in spoken-language AI is uncertain, and if human-to-human spoken fluency retains value the instrumental framework underweights, this rating could overstate the erosion.
FRE 2020.d: This course is a continuation of FRE 2010 and is the second of a two-semester, integrated, second-year sequence. The course focuses on further skills development in listening, speaking, reading, and writing, with emphasis on the use of functional, communicative language for oral and written proficiency and on cultural competency. Class is conducted mostly in French and will include a variety of interactive activities designed to help students develop their knowledge of French and their ability to use it productively in situations of communication.

r: French Reading and Conversation builds oral proficiency at intermediate and advanced levels through personalized interactional activities grounded in level-appropriate readings, a course whose center of gravity is live, real-time spoken interaction between students and instructor, more heavily weighted toward embodied conversation than the standard four-skills sequence. Task-exposure research still classifies translation and interpretation as highly exposed, pressuring the instrumental case downward when the task is narrowly linguistic transfer. But this course's explicit design around personalized, in-the-moment conversational exchange makes embodiment strongly protective here, triggering a downward adjustment beyond what the base task-exposure reading alone would suggest. It requires one year of college French, giving it modest sequence placement, though it does not gate further required coursework. At 24 months, the course's conversational core is untouched by translation-tool maturity. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI conversational-practice tools and real-time translation will be sophisticated enough to handle much of the reading-comprehension and vocabulary-support work this course assigns, and observed-usage data confirms language and writing tasks are already common AI applications. That pushes the base exposure reading toward Medium or higher. What continues to protect the course is its explicit emphasis on live, personalized spoken interaction, an embodied, real-time component that a translation or chatbot tool does not replicate in a classroom conversation-practice setting. That embodiment factor is strong enough to hold the rating at Medium rather than allowing it to climb to High, even without a GT-Pathways designation or strong prerequisite lock. The instrumental case weakens for the reading-comprehension component but persists for the conversational core. Rating: Medium.

A decade out, AI conversational agents capable of naturalistic spoken interaction are a plausible central-case development, which would narrow the gap between AI-mediated and human conversation practice somewhat. Even so, the course's pedagogical premise, that a student needs personalized, real-time interactional practice with another speaker to build oral proficiency, retains protective weight under the embodiment factor, holding the rating at Medium rather than High. Task-exposure research's placement of translation-adjacent work high on the exposure scale continues to weigh against the course's reading-support component. Confidence here is lower than for most catalog courses: whether advanced conversational AI at this horizon meaningfully substitutes for live human conversation practice is genuinely unsettled, and this is exactly the kind of judgment call where the embodiment protection could prove weaker than the rating assumes. Rating: Medium.
FRE 2110.d: This course helps to build oral proficiency at intermediate and advanced levels through a variety of personalized interactional activities that are based on readings appropriate to each stage of linguistic development.

r: This variable-credit course recognizes a second-year approved study-abroad experience in French language and culture, crediting sustained immersive engagement rather than classroom instruction. As with its first-year counterpart, the applied activity is embodied, real-time presence in a francophone environment, navigating daily life, academic work, and social relationships in the language, placing it in the lowest-exposure category task-exposure research identifies for physical, in-person, interpersonal work. A one-year college French prerequisite indicates advancing proficiency, but the course's instrumental function is the immersion itself, not a transferable cross-language task an AI system could intercept. No degree of machine-translation capability substitutes for physically living and studying in a French-speaking setting. At 24 months, the instrumental requirement for immersive presence to earn this credit is fully intact. Rating: Low.

By 2031, real-time AI translation will likely be a routine travel and study aid, potentially easing daily communication friction for students abroad. That convenience, however, does not substitute for the credited activity itself: sustained embodied immersion in a francophone academic and cultural environment. Embodiment and verification factors sit near their protective floor for this course, consistent with the jagged-frontier finding that AI assistance functions very differently for in-person, real-time interpersonal contexts than for digital knowledge work, and with task-exposure research's low-exposure classification for physically-present activity. Diffusion of ambient translation tools changes how immersion feels but does not remove the requirement of physical presence that the credit recognizes. The instrumental case for the course remains essentially intact at this horizon. Rating: Low.

A decade out, pervasive AI translation could make daily functioning abroad easier without deep language study, a genuine downward pressure task-exposure research would flag for translation-dependent tasks generally. But this course does not credit translation competence; it credits an embodied, sustained immersion experience that inherently requires physical presence in a francophone setting, something no plausible AI capability trajectory eliminates, however far real-time interpretation advances. The central case still has advancing French students living and studying abroad to earn this credit, protected by the same embodiment logic that holds at 24 months and five years. Rating: Low, with lower-than-typical confidence reflecting the thin, generic variable-credit description rather than any real doubt about the structural protection embodiment provides for immersive study abroad experiences of this kind.
FRE 2800.d: This is a variable-credit course that recognizes second- year study of French language and culture in an approved study- abroad setting.

r: This transitional upper-division course develops the critical, linguistic, and analytical skills needed to pursue advanced French studies, working through literary texts, films, news, and audio and video sources to examine Francophone socio-cultural and literary issues. The applied work here shifts from raw communicative-skill building toward textual and media analysis and critical synthesis in French, tasks task-exposure research associates with higher exposure given AI's strength in writing, synthesis, and language-adjacent reasoning, though foreign-language comprehension still carries some of the translation-exposure logic affecting the broader sequence. The course carries no GT-Pathways designation, but it functions as the required gateway into advanced French coursework, giving it real scaffolding weight. At 24 months, near-term classroom diffusion of AI analytical tools into upper-division language study is still partial, and the prerequisite role keeps enrollment instrumentally necessary. Rating: Medium.

By 2031, AI will competently perform much of the critical reading, cross-media synthesis, and analytical writing about literary and cultural sources that this course assigns, consistent with task-exposure research's strong positive association between exposure and writing and synthesis work. The course's foundational-scaffolding protection, which caps the rating at Medium, applies only at the 24-month horizon under the deterministic rule and lapses by five years; with no GT-Pathways designation and no accreditation-level lock, little structural protection remains. Verification burden is moderate rather than high, misreadings of literary nuance are consequential to scholarship but not adversarial or safety-critical, so the dampening factor does not apply either. The instrumental case for a student personally producing this level of textual and cultural analysis substantially erodes. Rating: High.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating fluent literary and cultural analysis across French-language sources on demand, extending the trajectory already visible in five-year capability projections. With no institutional lock beyond the course's internal role as a gateway to further French study, a program-level requirement the rubric treats as weak protection once the 24-month scaffolding cap lapses, little holds the rating below High. The instrumental case for a student to personally develop these critical and analytical skills, rather than relying on AI-generated synthesis, is substantially eroded under the central capability trajectory. Rating: High, hedged meaningfully: ten-year forecasts for foreign-language critical analysis are uncertain, and if reading comprehension and critical judgment in a second language retain value AI cannot fully replicate, the true erosion could be less than this rating implies.
FRE 3010.d: This transitional course is designed to develop those critical, linguistic, and analytical skills required to pursue French studies at the advanced level. The cultural sources studied-literary texts, films, news articles, videos, audio programs, etc.- are chosen to acquaint students with Francophone socio-cultural and literary issues.

r: Cultural Crossroads examines heritage languages and cultures in the United States: language families, the historical and geopolitical drivers of emigration, the formation of immigrant diasporas, differing social etiquette in cross-cultural exchange, and the role heritage languages play in shaping identity and community. The prerequisite is ENG 1020 rather than any French course, so instruction and assessed writing occur in English; the applied work is humanities synthesis and analytical discussion, not French-language production or translation. Task-exposure research finds writing and synthesis positively associated with AI exposure, and observed-usage data shows office and writing tasks already dominate consumer AI use, pushing the base rating toward Medium even this early. Unlike several French offerings, this course carries no GT-Pathways designation, so no institutional mandate anchors it, and nothing in its content is foundational scaffolding for further required coursework. Rating: Medium.

By 2031, AI systems will competently draft the kind of cultural comparison, historical synthesis, and diaspora analysis this course assigns, and productivity research on professional writing, faster output paired with quality gains, suggests students will lean heavily on such tools for these deliverables. Because the course requires no French-language production, embodiment offers no protection here, unlike the conversational and phonetics-focused French courses in this catalog; the work is fully digital, text-based humanities analysis. With no GT-Pathways designation and no downstream prerequisite role, neither institutional lock-in nor foundational scaffolding restrains the rating once base exposure rises. Task-exposure research's positive association between writing tasks and AI exposure, combined with the absence of any structural protection present for other French offerings, supports a rise to High. The instrumental case for a student personally producing this analysis substantially erodes. Rating: High, with moderate confidence given the generic, survey-style course description.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating fluent cross-cultural, historical, and sociolinguistic synthesis on demand, comparable to how general-education humanities surveys read elsewhere in this framework: no embodiment, no verification-critical stakes, and no accreditation lock. The instrumental rationale for a student to personally produce comparative analysis of heritage-language communities is substantially eroded under the central capability trajectory, and unlike courses anchored by a GT-Pathways designation, nothing here keeps the rating from tracking base exposure upward. Rating holds High rather than climbing further only because the deterministic rule has already reached its ceiling; there is no additional headroom. Confidence is moderate-to-low: ten-year forecasts for how elective cultural-studies courses are taught and assessed under ubiquitous AI are inherently uncertain, and if disciplinary norms shift toward oral presentation or fieldwork-style engagement, some embodied protection could reappear that this rating does not currently capture.
FRE 3050.d: Cultural Crossroads focuses on heritage languages and cultures in the USA. Students gain the cultural background necessary for insightful interaction with the rich diversity of heritage languages and cultures present in the United States. Main topics include the variety of language families, the historical and geo-political reasons for emigration, the establishment and treatment of immigrant diasporas, the role of differing social etiquette in cultural exchanges, the contributions of immigrants to their new country, and the importance of heritage languages in shaping identities, communities, and society.

r: French Legacies I surveys France from prehistoric origins through Louis XIV, using primary sources, visual culture, literature, and foundational texts to examine Paleolithic art, Celtic migrations, Romanization, the Carolingian Renaissance, Gothic architecture, the Hundred Years' War, and Renaissance humanism. Requiring FRE 3010, the course is conducted with substantial French-language engagement, and the applied work is critical reading, historical synthesis, and analytical writing about primary and literary sources, tasks task-exposure research links to higher exposure given AI's demonstrated strength in writing and synthesis. The course carries no GT-Pathways designation, and while FRE 3010 gates entry, French Legacies I does not itself gate any later required course; it is one of three independently offered topical courses on French cultural history. At 24 months, near-term classroom diffusion into upper-division literary-historical study remains partial, keeping the instrumental case at Medium.

By 2031, AI will competently perform much of the critical reading, cross-source synthesis, and analytical writing about medieval and early-modern French visual culture and literature that this course assigns, consistent with task-exposure research's positive association between writing and synthesis work and AI exposure. Because French Legacies I carries no GT-Pathways designation and does not itself gate further required coursework, no structural protection restrains the rating once base exposure rises with capability. Verification burden is moderate rather than high; misreadings of historical or literary nuance are consequential to scholarship but not adversarial or safety-critical, so the dampening factor does not apply. The instrumental case for a student personally producing this level of historical-literary analysis in French substantially erodes at this horizon. Rating: High, reflecting the absence of any institutional anchor comparable to those protecting general-education French offerings.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating fluent historical and literary analysis of French sources across any period on demand, extending the trajectory already visible in five-year capability projections. With no GT-Pathways designation and no role gating further required coursework beyond the FRE 3010 prerequisite already satisfied to enroll, little structural protection remains once the deterministic rule's caps lapse. The instrumental case for a student to personally develop the critical-reading and analytical-writing competence this course builds, rather than relying on AI-generated synthesis of primary and literary sources, is substantially eroded under the central capability trajectory. Rating: High, hedged meaningfully: ten-year forecasts for foreign-language critical-historical analysis are uncertain, and if close reading of primary sources in a second language retains pedagogical value AI cannot fully replicate, the true erosion could be less than this rating implies.
FRE 3110.d: In this course, students engage in a historical and cultural survey of France from its prehistoric origins through the reign of Louis XIV. Students explore major developments that shaped French identity, from Paleolithic art and Celtic migrations to Romanization, Christianization, and the shaping of a medieval society of hierarchical orders. Key moments such as the Carolingian Renaissance, the rise of Gothic architecture, the Hundred Years' War, and the Renaissance humanist movement are studied through visual culture, literature, and foundational texts. Special emphasis is placed on the evolution of the French language, key historical myths, and France's early global ambitions. Through a variety of primary sources, students gain insight into the artistic, political, religious, and intellectual currents that defined early France.

r: French Legacies II surveys France from the Enlightenment to the 1920s, examining sociopolitical satire, cultural and geographic expansion, and industrialization through the first encyclopedia, the Declaration of the Rights of Man, the Napoleonic Code, the Romantic movement, the advent of the railway, and movements for equality and social justice, using primary sources, visual culture, and literature. Requiring FRE 3010, the applied work is critical reading, historical synthesis, and analytical writing in French about these primary and literary sources, tasks task-exposure research links to higher exposure given AI's strength in writing and synthesis. The course carries no GT-Pathways designation, and although FRE 3010 gates entry, French Legacies II does not itself gate any later required course; it stands as one of three independently offered topical courses. At 24 months, near-term diffusion into upper-division literary-historical French study remains partial, keeping the instrumental case at Medium.

By 2031, AI will competently perform much of the critical reading, cross-source synthesis, and analytical writing about Enlightenment-to-interwar French political, legal, and cultural history that this course assigns, consistent with task-exposure research's positive association between writing and synthesis work and AI exposure. Because French Legacies II carries no GT-Pathways designation and does not itself gate further required coursework, no structural protection restrains the rating once base exposure rises with capability. Verification burden is moderate rather than high; misreadings of a primary source's historical significance are consequential to scholarship but not adversarial or safety-critical, so the dampening factor does not apply. The instrumental case for a student personally producing this level of historical-literary analysis in French substantially erodes at this horizon. Rating: High, reflecting the absence of any institutional anchor comparable to those protecting general-education French offerings elsewhere.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating fluent political, legal, and cultural-historical analysis of French sources across the Enlightenment-to-interwar period on demand, extending the trajectory already visible in five-year projections. With no GT-Pathways designation and no role gating further required coursework beyond the FRE 3010 prerequisite already satisfied to enroll, little structural protection remains once the deterministic rule's caps lapse. The instrumental case for a student to personally develop the critical-reading and analytical-writing competence this course builds, rather than relying on AI-generated synthesis of primary and literary sources, is substantially eroded under the central capability trajectory. Rating: High, hedged meaningfully: ten-year forecasts for foreign-language critical-historical analysis are uncertain, and if close reading of primary sources in a second language retains pedagogical value AI cannot fully replicate, the true erosion could be less than this rating implies.
FRE 3120.d: In this course, students engage in a historical and cultural survey of France from the Enlightenment to the 1920s. Students explore major developments that shaped French identity such as socio-political satire, cultural and geographic expansion, and the industrial revolution. Key moments such as the creation of the first encyclopedia, the Declaration of the Rights of Man, the Napoleonic Code, the Romantic movement, and the advent of the railway are studied through visual culture, literature, and foundational texts. Special emphasis is placed on diverse movements for equality and social justice, key historical myths, and France's continued global expansion. Through a variety of primary sources, students gain insight into the artistic, political, religious, and intellectual currents that defined 18th and 19th-century France.

r: French Legacies III surveys France from the Second World War to the present, examining existentialism, feminism, and post-colonial movements through the Nazi occupation and liberation, Algerian independence, the protests of May 1968, and contemporary sociopolitical movements, using primary sources, visual culture, and literature. Requiring FRE 3010, the applied work is critical reading, historical synthesis, and analytical writing in French about these sources, tasks task-exposure research links to higher exposure given AI's demonstrated strength in writing and synthesis. The course carries no GT-Pathways designation, and although FRE 3010 gates entry, French Legacies III does not itself gate any later required course; it is one of three independently offered topical courses covering different periods of French history. At 24 months, near-term diffusion into upper-division literary-historical French study remains partial, keeping the instrumental case at Medium.

By 2031, AI will competently perform much of the critical reading, cross-source synthesis, and analytical writing about postwar French intellectual, political, and social movements that this course assigns, consistent with task-exposure research's positive association between writing and synthesis work and AI exposure. Because French Legacies III carries no GT-Pathways designation and does not itself gate further required coursework, no structural protection restrains the rating once base exposure rises with capability. Verification burden is moderate rather than high; misreadings of a text's political or philosophical stance are consequential to scholarship but not adversarial or safety-critical, so the dampening factor does not apply. The instrumental case for a student personally producing this level of historical-literary analysis in French substantially erodes at this horizon. Rating: High, reflecting the absence of any institutional anchor comparable to those protecting general-education French offerings elsewhere.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating fluent intellectual, political, and cultural-historical analysis of postwar French sources on demand, extending the trajectory already visible in five-year capability projections. With no GT-Pathways designation and no role gating further required coursework beyond the FRE 3010 prerequisite already satisfied to enroll, little structural protection remains once the deterministic rule's caps lapse. The instrumental case for a student to personally develop the critical-reading and analytical-writing competence this course builds, rather than relying on AI-generated synthesis of primary and literary sources, is substantially eroded under the central capability trajectory. Rating: High, hedged meaningfully: ten-year forecasts for foreign-language critical-historical analysis are uncertain, and if close reading of primary sources on contested political history retains pedagogical value AI cannot fully replicate, the true erosion could be less than this rating implies.
FRE 3130.d: In this course, students engage in a historical and cultural survey of France from the Second World War to present day. Students explore major cultural developments that shaped French identity such as existentialism, feminism, and post-colonial movements. Key moments such as the Nazi occupation and liberation of France, the Algerian independence, the protests of May 1968 and contemporary socio-political movements are studied through visual culture, literature, and foundational texts. Through a variety of primary sources, students gain insight into the artistic, political, religious, and intellectual currents that define contemporary France.

r: French Phonetics covers the essential facts of French phonology, aimed at improving students' pronunciation and articulation while introducing them to linguistics. The applied work is embodied, real-time oral practice: producing and refining French sounds under instructor feedback, a psychomotor and auditory skill closer to the low-exposure interpersonal categories task-exposure research identifies than to text-based language tasks. Requiring two years of college French, the course targets a student's own articulatory competence rather than a translatable or transcribable product an AI system could substitute. The embodiment factor triggers the deterministic dampener, dropping what would otherwise be a Medium base rating to Low even at 24 months. The course carries no GT-Pathways designation and does not gate further required coursework, so no institutional or scaffolding cap independently applies; embodiment alone is doing the protective work here. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI speech-analysis and pronunciation-feedback tools will be considerably more capable, and observed-usage data confirms language tasks are already common AI applications, pushing the base F1 rating toward High as automated phonetic tools mature and diffuse. But the course's core purpose, a student developing personal articulatory control and auditory discrimination through live, embodied practice, is not a task AI performs on the learner's behalf; a tool can model correct pronunciation, but it cannot build the student's own psychomotor competence. The embodiment dampener continues to apply, pulling the rating down one band from the rising base. With no GT-Pathways designation and no downstream gating role, embodiment is again the sole protective factor, but it is sufficient. Rating: Medium, reflecting genuinely higher underlying exposure offset by the embodied nature of the skill itself.

A decade out, AI pronunciation coaching and phonetic-transcription tools will likely be excellent and widely diffused, and the descriptive-linguistics component of the course, transcribing and analyzing sound systems, could be substantially handled by such tools. But the embodied core, a student personally producing and refining articulate French speech, remains protected by the same embodiment logic that holds at earlier horizons; no plausible AI capability trajectory performs a learner's own oral practice for them. With no GT-Pathways designation or foundational-scaffolding cap doing additional work, embodiment alone continues to hold the rating at Medium rather than High. Confidence is moderate: the balance between phonetic theory, which is more automatable, and hands-on articulation practice, which is not, could shift the course's emphasis in ways this rating does not fully anticipate over a ten-year horizon.
FRE 3150.d: This course covers the essential facts of French phonology. It is aimed at improving students' pronunciation and articulation and introducing them to the field of linguistics.

r: Advanced French Composition and Grammar reinforces and develops writing skills so students can combine accuracy with imagination and inventiveness in written French. The applied work is text production and revision, exactly the category task-exposure research finds strongly and positively associated with AI exposure, and productivity research on professional writing shows large speed and quality gains from AI drafting assistance. Requiring FRE 2010 and FRE 2020, the course builds writing competence used across upper-division French study, but it is not itself listed as a formal prerequisite for other courses in the catalog, so its scaffolding role is real but not critical. The course carries no GT-Pathways designation, unlike some general-education French offerings, removing that institutional anchor. At 24 months, near-term classroom adoption of AI drafting tools for graded French composition remains partial, keeping the instrumental case at Medium rather than higher.

By 2031, AI writing tools will fluently draft and revise polished, idiomatic French prose on demand, sharply challenging the rationale for teaching students to compose it by hand; writing ranks among the most-exposed tasks in the evidence base, and language models already handle grammar and style refinement well in French as in English. The instrumental case shifts toward a student's ability to direct, evaluate, and revise AI-generated French writing, a real skill but a diminished version of the course's original composition-focused aim. With no GT-Pathways designation and only a weak, non-gating scaffolding role, no structural protection caps the rating once base exposure rises. Verification burden remains moderate rather than high, since grammatical errors in student writing are low-stakes and easily checked. Rating: High, reflecting writing's position as one of the most AI-exposed task categories with minimal institutional counterweight.

A decade out, AI French writing is pervasive, grammatically flawless, and stylistically fluent, and the central case has the raw composition task fully automated. The residual instrumental value lies in a student's own capacity to reason and express nuance in written French and to evaluate AI-generated prose for accuracy and register, a real but narrower rationale than the course's traditional composition-and-grammar framing. With no GT-Pathways mandate and no critical gating role for later required coursework, nothing structurally holds the rating below High once base exposure peaks. Rating: High, hedged considerably: forecasting how composition pedagogy evolves once AI writes fluent French by default is uncertain, and if the French program restructures such courses toward oversight and stylistic judgment rather than production, some of that residual value could be underweighted in this instrumental-need framework.
FRE 3310.d: This course is designed to reinforce and further develop writing skills, thus enabling the student to combine accuracy with imagination and inventiveness in writing French.

r: Cinema in French for Advanced Conversation uses French-language films as a vehicle for advanced comprehension and expression, encouraging students to use sophisticated grammatical structures and idiomatic expressions in live discussion. Despite the film-viewing content, the graded competence is real-time spoken conversation, embodied, interpersonal, and improvisational, placing it in the low-exposure categories task-exposure research reserves for in-person interaction rather than text production. Requiring FRE 3010 or senior standing, the course targets a student's own oral fluency, which no AI system substitutes for in a live classroom discussion setting. The embodiment factor triggers the deterministic dampener, dropping what would otherwise be a Medium base rating to Low at 24 months. With no GT-Pathways designation and no gating role for later required courses, embodiment alone provides the protection here, but it is sufficient. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI film-analysis and conversational-practice tools will be considerably more capable, and observed-usage data confirms language and media-analysis tasks are already common AI applications, pushing the base rating toward High as tools that summarize films or model idiomatic phrasing mature. But the graded work in this course is the student's own live, real-time conversation about the films, not written analysis, and no AI system performs a student's spoken participation in a discussion-based classroom. The embodiment dampener continues to apply, pulling the rating down one band from the rising base. With no GT-Pathways designation or downstream gating role, embodiment remains the sole but sufficient protective factor. Rating: Medium, reflecting genuinely higher underlying exposure in the film-comprehension component offset by the embodied, conversational core the course is actually built around.

A decade out, AI systems will summarize and analyze French cinema fluently and could plausibly generate convincing simulated conversation practice, and the film-comprehension groundwork this course builds becomes substantially automatable. But the course's actual center of gravity, a student developing spoken fluency through live, unscripted classroom conversation, remains protected by the same embodiment logic that holds at earlier horizons; a discussion is graded on a student's real-time participation, not a document AI could produce. With no GT-Pathways designation or foundational-scaffolding cap doing additional work, embodiment alone continues to hold the rating at Medium rather than High. Confidence is moderate: if the course shifts emphasis toward written film criticism as film-comprehension automates, the balance could tip further toward exposure than this rating currently reflects.
FRE 3320.d: This course explores French-language films and provides a vehicle for advanced-level French language comprehension and expression. While students receive an enriched understanding of contemporary French culture, they are encouraged to use advanced structures of the language, as well as other aspects of grammar and idiomatic expressions.

r: Special Topics in French Cultures has students critically engage a broad sampling of French and Francophone cultural production, graphic novels, detective fiction, music, and other popular culture alongside new historical perspectives, conducted entirely in French. The applied work is reading, viewing, discussing, and writing critical responses to varied cultural texts, tasks task-exposure research links to higher exposure given AI's demonstrated strength in synthesis and writing across genres. Requiring only FRE 2020, the course is a repeatable, topic-varying elective that neither carries a GT-Pathways designation nor gates any later required French course, so no institutional or scaffolding protection applies. At 24 months, near-term classroom diffusion of AI cultural-analysis and writing tools into this kind of varied-topics seminar remains partial, keeping the instrumental case at Medium rather than higher, though with little structural anchor to prevent further erosion.

By 2031, AI will fluently read, summarize, and critically analyze graphic novels, detective fiction, music, and popular culture across genres in French, consistent with task-exposure research's positive association between writing and synthesis tasks and AI exposure. Because the course is a repeatable topics seminar with no GT-Pathways designation and no gating role for other required coursework, no structural protection restrains the rating once base exposure rises with capability. Verification burden is moderate rather than high; a student's or AI's interpretation of a cultural text is a scholarly judgment call, not an adversarial or safety-critical determination, so the dampening factor does not apply. The instrumental case for a student personally producing this critical cultural analysis substantially erodes. Rating: High, reflecting the course's high content-exposure and its complete lack of institutional or scaffolding anchor.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating sophisticated critical readings of popular and literary French-language culture across whatever genres a given semester's topics offering covers, extending the five-year trajectory. With no GT-Pathways designation and no role gating further required coursework, nothing structurally holds the rating below High once base exposure peaks. The instrumental case for a student to personally produce critical analysis of graphic novels, genre fiction, or music in French, rather than relying on AI-generated cultural criticism, is substantially eroded under the central capability trajectory. Rating: High, hedged meaningfully: ten-year forecasts for how varied-topics humanities seminars are taught and assessed under ubiquitous AI are uncertain, and if the course leans further into live discussion and debate as written analysis automates, some embodied protection could reappear that this rating does not capture.
FRE 3600.d: Students discover and engage critically with a broad sampling of French and Francophone cultural production. Students read, watch, write about, and discuss a variety of works that may include graphic novels, detective fiction, music, and other forms of popular culture, as well as new historical perspectives. The topics vary from semester to semester. The course is conducted entirely in French.

r: Introduction to French Translation is the catalog's most direct translation course: students translate texts between French and English, critique translations, examine translation theory, analyze grammatical, lexical, and cultural issues, research terminology, and learn the technical, business, and ethical dimensions of freelance translation. Task-exposure research places translators and interpreters among the single most AI-exposed occupations in the evidence base, and the course's applied work, converting meaning between languages in written text, is precisely that occupational activity with no embodied or real-time component to protect it. Requiring only FRE 2020, the course carries no GT-Pathways designation and gates no other required coursework. At 24 months, machine translation already performs competently on much of the routine translation work this course teaches; the base rating starts at High, and no structural factor pulls it down. Rating: High.

By 2031, AI translation systems will handle the great majority of routine French-English and English-French text conversion with high fluency, deepening the erosion task-exposure research already flags for translators as an occupational category. The course's remaining value shifts toward the theoretical, cultural, and terminological judgment that distinguishes competent human translation from literal machine output, a genuine residual competence, but the instrumental case for taking a course to build routine translation skill is substantially eroded. Verification burden stays moderate, translation errors are correctable and rarely catastrophic in this context, so no dampener applies, and with no GT-Pathways designation or gating role, no institutional cap restrains the rating either. Rating: High, essentially unchanged from 24 months because the course's core task was already near the ceiling of AI exposure even before this horizon.

A decade out, seamless AI translation at native-speaker quality is the central-case expectation, and the instrumental rationale for a dedicated undergraduate course teaching translation mechanics is close to fully displaced by capability alone. What survives is professional judgment about register, cultural nuance, and ethical practice in contexts where a client specifically requires human accountability, a narrow niche rather than a broad instrumental need. No GT-Pathways designation, no accreditation lock, and no gating role for other coursework leave nothing to hold the rating below High. Rating: High, held with only moderate confidence: this is precisely the occupation task-exposure research most consistently flags as automatable, so the direction is not in serious doubt, though the pace at which undergraduate translation instruction itself disappears or repositions toward AI-oversight skills remains genuinely uncertain over a ten-year horizon.
FRE 3650.d: This course is an introduction to the principal topics in the discipline of translation. The student translates a variety of texts from French to English and from English to French, discusses and critiques translations in class, examines various theoretical concepts of translation, and analyzes grammatical, lexical and cultural issues faced by translators. The student also identifies fundamental issues specific to various translation domains, develops essential skills for researching terminology, and translates texts from those areas. The student is familiarized with the technical, business and ethical sides of freelance translation.

r: International Advanced French recognizes upper-division study in language, culture, and literature undertaken in a study-abroad setting, crediting reading, writing, and discussion seminars conducted in French within an immersive environment. The applied work is embodied, real-time engagement with the language and culture, navigating academic and daily life abroad, activities task-exposure research places in the low-exposure category reserved for physical, in-person work rather than text-based tasks a translation tool could intercept. Requiring at least junior standing in French, the course's instrumental function is the immersion experience itself, not a transferable digital task. No GT-Pathways designation or downstream gating role exists, but embodiment alone triggers the deterministic dampener, holding the rating at Low even before considering any institutional cap. At 24 months, the requirement for a student to be physically present abroad to earn this credit is entirely untouched by AI capability. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI translation apps will be routine travel companions, potentially reducing daily communication friction for students abroad, but that convenience does not substitute for the credited activity: sustained immersive study within a francophone academic and cultural environment at an advanced level. The embodiment and verification factors sit near their protective floor for this course, consistent with the jagged-frontier finding that AI assistance functions very differently for in-person, real-time interpersonal contexts than for digital knowledge work, and with task-exposure research's low-exposure classification for physically present activity. Diffusion of ambient translation tools changes how immersion feels day to day but does not remove the requirement of physical presence the credit recognizes. Because embodiment alone already pulls the rating down regardless of a rising base, the instrumental case for the course remains essentially intact. Rating: Low.

A decade out, pervasive AI translation could make daily functioning abroad easier without deep language study, a genuine downward pressure task-exposure research would flag for translation-dependent tasks generally. But this course does not credit translation competence; it credits an embodied, sustained, advanced-level immersion experience that inherently requires physical presence in a francophone setting, something no plausible AI capability trajectory eliminates, however far real-time interpretation advances. The central case still has advanced French students living and studying abroad to earn this credit, protected by the same embodiment logic that holds at earlier horizons. Rating: Low, with lower-than-typical confidence reflecting the thin, generic variable-credit description rather than any real doubt about the structural protection embodiment provides for immersive study-abroad experiences of this kind at the advanced level.
FRE 3800.d: This course recognizes upper-division study in language, culture, and literature in a study abroad setting. It uses a variety of methods and includes reading, writing, and discussion seminars in French.

r: FRE 4520 asks students to close-read French dramatic texts, evaluate playwrights' societal and cultural impact, and apply theater analysis techniques covering staging, characterization, and dramaturgical structure. Task-exposure research finds programming and writing skills strongly positively associated with exposure while critical-thinking skills are negatively associated, and current models can summarize canonical plays and draft basic thematic commentary but strain on culturally embedded staging analysis and historically grounded societal critique in French. Observed-usage data shows writing-adjacent tasks are heavily used, but that usage concentrates in English-language, general-purpose contexts rather than specialized French dramaturgy, so realized classroom substitution is limited. No GT-Pathways designation or accreditation mandate constrains this senior-standing elective, so no institutional lock-in currently protects it from automation pressure; the binding constraint instead is faculty expertise needed to verify culturally specific interpretive claims that current tools handle unevenly.

By 2031, task-time-horizon capability trends suggest models will handle longer, more coherent literary commentary, and adoption of AI writing assistants in humanities coursework is likely to grow beyond current levels, though Census BTOS diffusion data show firm-level AI use still uneven, implying classroom uptake lags capability. Drafting comparative essays on French dramatists and synthesizing theater analysis frameworks becomes more tractable for AI, nudging realized automatability into moderate territory. Verification burden remains real: the jagged-frontier finding that users misjudge accuracy outside a model's strong suit applies directly to nuanced staging interpretation and socio-historical framing, so faculty oversight stays necessary. No accreditation or GT lock-in emerges by this horizon. This is a moderate, not confident, projection given the specialized nature of French-language dramatic criticism and the thinness of adoption data specific to foreign-language literary seminars.

Ten-year projections carry substantial uncertainty. If the roughly four-to-seven-month doubling in model task-time-horizons continues, AI could plausibly draft full comparative analyses of French theater with reasonable coherence, and enterprise-style automation rates well above consumer levels could extend into instructional contexts. Yet Acemoglu-style macroeconomic estimates suggest aggregate productivity effects from AI remain modest over a decade, and diffusion into niche humanities instruction historically lags general-purpose capability by years. Interpretive judgment about societal impact and staging choices, which task-exposure research links to critical-thinking skills that resist automation, likely keeps a meaningful human role even as drafting support becomes routine. No licensure, GT, or accreditation constraint will emerge to protect this course structurally, so its resilience depends entirely on the durability of interpretive skill rather than institutional lock-in, a genuinely uncertain bet at this horizon.
FRE 4520.d: This is a sampling of the French dramatists who have not only contributed to literary development, but who also have had an impact on society and culture. Theater analysis techniques will also be stressed.

r: FRE 4530 requires close reading of nineteenth- and twentieth-century French novels using multiple literary analysis techniques, producing interpretive essays on theme, narrative structure, and historical context. Because this work is entirely textual, it sits closer to AI's current strengths than performance-based courses: task-exposure research classifies writing skills as strongly positively associated with exposure, and GDPval benchmarking shows top models already reaching roughly half of expert-level wins on real deliverable tasks, a meaningful though not decisive threshold for essay-style literary analysis. Observed-usage data confirms writing and office-style tasks dominate current AI use. Verification burden remains moderate rather than low, since accurate interpretation of French prose in original language still benefits from instructor review. No GT-Pathways designation or accreditation requirement locks this senior elective in place, leaving its near-term standing tied to realized rather than merely possible automatability.

Over the next several years, capability trends pointing to roughly four-to-seven-month doublings in model task-time-horizons suggest sustained essay drafting and multi-novel comparative analysis in French becomes increasingly reliable, pushing realized automatability higher. Productivity-RCT evidence on professional writing, where AI assistance cut time substantially while improving rated quality, is suggestive of how literary-essay drafting workflows could shift for students and instructors alike, though that evidence comes from professional rather than instructional settings. Diffusion remains uneven per Census BTOS figures, meaning classroom adoption will likely trail raw capability. The course carries no institutional lock-in, so nothing structurally protects it, and its trajectory depends on how thoroughly instructors integrate rather than resist AI drafting tools. This is a moderate-confidence, directional judgment rather than a firm prediction given limited direct evidence on undergraduate French literary coursework specifically.

A ten-year outlook is necessarily speculative. If capability growth documented by METR/Epoch continues compounding, AI systems could plausibly produce sophisticated comparative readings of French novels approaching expert quality, especially given GDPval's evidence that models are already closing in on human-expert performance on real deliverables. Because the course's core work, textual interpretation and essay production, is fully digital with no embodiment barrier, few structural verification obstacles would remain except reviewers checking language accuracy and originality. No accreditation, GT, or licensure mandate offers institutional protection at any horizon. Still, adoption diffusion has historically lagged capability by years, and aggregate productivity estimates over a decade stay modest, so confident claims about full instructional substitution by 2036 are unwarranted. The realistic expectation is high potential automatability tempered by genuine uncertainty about actual classroom deployment timing.
FRE 4530.d: This is a sampling of 19th- and 20th-century French novels that will be studied in depth using several literary analysis techniques.

r: FRE 4540 trains students to translate between French and English, analyze cultural differences shaping both textual and image-based translation, and complete a service-learning translation project with community reflection. Task-exposure research explicitly names translators and interpreters among the most-exposed occupational categories, and current machine translation quality already handles much routine French-English conversion competently, making this the most automatable of the department's upper-division offerings. However, the course's cultural-analysis component and its applied service-learning project with a real community partner retain an interpersonal, context-sensitive dimension that pure text translation lacks, moderating full automatability. Verification burden stays real: the jagged-frontier finding that users misjudge AI accuracy outside its strong suit applies to culturally loaded idiom and image-text translation choices. No GT designation or accreditation mandate protects this capped 15-student seminar, so its standing rests on task substitution dynamics already underway.

By 2031, given translation's position as one of the most AI-exposed task categories and continuing capability gains implied by shortening model task-time-horizons, routine French-English conversion work embedded in this course likely becomes substantially automatable, while cultural-analysis framing and the applied service-learning project retain a meaningful human component. Enterprise-style automation rates for language tasks, running well above consumer-level automation shares in current usage data, suggest institutions adopting AI translation tools at scale could reduce the instrumental need for manual translation drilling specifically. Diffusion remains uneven across firms per Census BTOS data, so the exact pace institutions adopt these tools for student translation projects is uncertain. The community-engaged reflection component is harder to automate than the translation mechanics themselves. This projection carries real uncertainty given how quickly institutional translation-pedagogy practice, as distinct from raw MT capability, will actually shift.

Ten years out, if translation continues to rank among the most AI-exposed task categories and capability compounds at rates consistent with recent trends, the mechanical French-English and English-French conversion work at this course's core plausibly becomes highly automatable, with AI handling most routine translation tasks competently. What resists this trajectory is the course's cultural and service-learning framing, since analyzing how cultural differences affect image and text translation, and completing a reflective community-engaged project, involve interpersonal judgment less amenable to full substitution even under optimistic capability assumptions. No accreditation or GT lock-in will emerge to protect the course structurally. Macro-level productivity estimates over a decade remain modest despite fast model progress, a reminder that capability and realized classroom substitution are distinct; the directional bet toward high automatability is reasonable but not a confident point prediction.
FRE 4540.d: This course is designed to allow students to use the various skills that they have developed during their studies of French language, culture and literature at an advanced level. Students analyze and apply translation techniques (from both French to English and English to French) and demonstrate an ability to analyze cultural differences that affect translation, both of text and image. The course provides a practical application of skills toward a service- learning translation project and includes reflection on the service learning process. Enrollment is limited to 15 students.

r: FRE 4750 is a capstone thematic seminar requiring comparative literary or cultural analysis, often multidisciplinary, on topics such as gender, women, and sexualities, synthesized from prior coursework at senior standing. Task-exposure research finds critical-thinking skills strongly negatively associated with AI exposure, and this course's core work, original comparative argumentation across texts and disciplines, sits squarely in that protected category rather than in the writing-heavy tasks positively associated with exposure. Verification burden is elevated because the capstone nature of the seminar means low tolerance for shallow or generic synthesis, and the jagged-frontier finding that users misjudge AI accuracy outside its strong suit is especially relevant to open-ended comparative argument. Observed-usage data confirms AI use concentrates in more routine writing tasks rather than original scholarly synthesis. No GT designation offers protection, but the course's intellectual demands currently do so instead.

By 2031, general model capability will likely improve on multidisciplinary synthesis given the pace suggested by shortening task-time-horizons, and drafting support for comparative seminar papers could become more common, moving realized automatability from low toward moderate. Still, task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking skills resist exposure argues against a sharp jump, since the course's value lies in original comparative framing across literary and cultural material rather than in producing polished prose alone. Diffusion data show AI adoption remains uneven across institutions, and capstone seminars are exactly the setting where faculty are likely to maintain close oversight given accreditation-adjacent expectations around original student work. No GT-Pathways or accreditation mandate applies here, so any resilience is a function of task difficulty rather than institutional protection. This moderate projection carries meaningful uncertainty given how seminar-format capstones evolve pedagogically alongside AI tools.

A ten-year horizon for a comparative capstone seminar is difficult to forecast with confidence. Continued capability growth along METR/Epoch-documented trends could narrow the gap on multidisciplinary synthesis, and GDPval-style benchmarks suggest models are approaching, though still below, expert-level performance on complex real-world deliverables. Task-exposure research's consistent finding that critical-thinking skills are negatively associated with exposure suggests the seminar's comparative-argument core remains relatively resistant even as drafting support becomes routine elsewhere in the curriculum. Aggregate productivity estimates over a decade stay modest, and diffusion into capstone-level humanities pedagogy specifically has no direct evidence base in the available research. No accreditation, licensure, or GT constraint will emerge to protect this course structurally. The most defensible position is continued moderate rather than high automatability, driven by the durability of original comparative reasoning rather than institutional lock-in.
FRE 4750.d: This is an intense thematic seminar on either a literary or cultural topic emphasizing a comparative study in the former and a multidisciplinary approach to the latter. Gender, Women and Sexualities
